rationale: The book establishes that Jerusalem can be symbolized as a harlot and that Revelation 11:8 calls the city of the crucifixion “the great city.” It does not establish that every occurrence of “the great city” in Revelation has the same referent. In Revelation 17, the woman is identified as the city then reigning over the kings of the earth and is associated with seven mountains; those details fit imperial Rome substantially better than first-century Jerusalem. Revelation 18’s international commerce, luxury, maritime traffic, and influence over kings likewise fit Rome’s imperial economy. The book’s proposed mediation—Jerusalem’s covenant order riding a western bloc of seven mountains—requires several speculative symbolic and lexical steps and still does not adequately explain how Jerusalem itself reigned over earthly kings. Moreover, the claim that only covenant people can be called harlots is weakened by the prophetic use of harlot imagery for Nineveh and Tyre. Rome therefore provides the stronger specific identification, while Jerusalem remains a genuine secondary echo supplied by the Old Testament harlot tradition and Revelation 11.
book_core_identification: The great harlot/Babylon of Revelation 17–18 is unfaithful Jerusalem, understood as the covenant order retaining covenant form while betraying its substance.
book_secondary_elaborations: Jerusalem bears the spiritual names Sodom, Egypt, and Babylon because of its sin, bondage, and boastfulness.
Aaron’s rod becoming a serpent depicts the priesthood or covenant order becoming dragon-like and riding the beast.
The seven mountains are a western bloc of nations ridden or dominated by the apostate covenant city.
Jeremiah’s “hindermost of the nations” identifies Babylon’s base of power with the far west.
The Exodus plagues, Moses’ signs, Babylon’s sinking, and Revelation’s judgments form one detailed end-time similitude.
The forehead name of the harlot is a counterfeit covenantal inscription.
Seizing the serpent by the tail symbolizes mastering lying prophetic leadership and restoring the priesthood.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The harlot Babylon in Revelation 17–18 is imperial Rome: the first-century city ruling over kings, conventionally associated with seven hills, enriched by international trade, implicated in imperial idolatry, and responsible for persecuting God’s people. Revelation 11:8 refers separately to Jerusalem as another “great city,” so its explicit crucifixion address need not identify the woman in Revelation 17.
counter_core_identification: The great harlot/Babylon of Revelation 17–18 is imperial Rome rather than Jerusalem.
material_core_denial: The shared descriptive phrase “great city” does not make Revelation 11’s Jerusalem identical with Revelation 17–18’s Babylon; the latter’s ruling position, seven mountains, imperial alliances, and global commerce identify Rome more naturally.
counter_case: Revelation 17:18 describes the woman as the city that reigns over the kings of the earth, an immediately recognizable description of imperial Rome but not first-century Jerusalem.
Revelation 17:9’s seven mountains strongly evokes Rome’s famous seven hills, whereas the book converts them into a western geopolitical bloc through an unsupported additional construction.
Revelation 17’s relations with kings, beastly imperial power, and persecution fit Rome’s political and cultic order without requiring Jerusalem secretly to control that order.
Revelation 18’s kings, merchants, luxury goods, seaborne trade, and worldwide economic collapse fit an imperial commercial center better than Jerusalem.
Revelation 11:8 explicitly supplies Jerusalem’s address only for the city in that vision; “great city” is descriptive rather than necessarily a unique proper name, having also been used for Nineveh.
The prophetic application of harlot imagery to Nineveh and Tyre shows that a harlot need not be a previously covenanted wife; an idolatrous, seductive imperial city can bear the image.
Rome as Babylon is independently consistent with early Christian use of “Babylon” as a cryptic designation for Rome, as in 1 Peter 5:13.
book_explanatory_advantages: It takes seriously Revelation 11:8’s explicit identification of a “great city” with the place where Jesus was crucified.
It integrates Revelation with Isaiah 1:21 and Ezekiel 16 and 23, where Jerusalem is expressly portrayed as a harlot.
It gives a strong intertextual explanation for the names Sodom and Egypt as judgments on Jerusalem’s conduct.
It connects Revelation 18:24’s blood of prophets and saints with Jesus’ accusations against Jerusalem in Matthew 23:35–37 and Luke 13:33.
It explains why harlot imagery carries overtones of religious betrayal rather than merely political oppression.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It directly fits Revelation 17:18’s present-tense picture of a city ruling earthly kings.
It explains the seven mountains by a prominent, historically intelligible feature of Rome without the book’s multi-stage geopolitical symbolism.
It accounts naturally for the beast, kings, imperial cult, persecution, wealth, merchants, and maritime economy as parts of one Roman imperial system.
It permits Revelation 11’s Jerusalem and Revelation 17’s Rome to be distinct cities rather than assuming that a recurring generic title fixes a single referent.
It accommodates the broader prophetic precedent of pagan commercial and imperial cities being called harlots.
It requires fewer speculative links than the book’s rod-serpent-priesthood, compass-word, western-bloc, and lying-tail constructions.
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Revelation 17:18 says that the woman’s city reigns over the kings of the earth. Jerusalem did not exercise such rule in the relevant first-century setting; treating an apostate Jerusalem-based covenant order as the hidden ruler of a western imperial bloc changes the ordinary historical referent and lacks direct textual support.

The combined portrait of seven mountains, imperial kings, worldwide luxury commerce, merchants, and maritime traffic coheres with Rome, while identifying the city as Jerusalem leaves these features dependent on an unexpressed transnational-control theory.
unresolved_objections: Revelation 18:24 and Jesus’ accusations against Jerusalem create a significant Jerusalem echo that a purely Roman reading must explain as typology, transferred guilt, or imperial complicity.
The harlot’s contrast with God’s faithful people gives the image covenantal force even if Rome is the historical referent.
Apocalyptic symbols can be polyvalent, so Rome may function as the immediate embodiment of a broader Babylonian world system rather than exhausting the symbol.
The supplied excerpts do not reproduce every verse of Revelation 17–18, limiting close evaluation of all details in their immediate context.
